# slide10
int Type Size Specifiers
Specifying the size of an int ensures that the type contains a minimum number of bits. The three specifiers are:
short: at least 16 bits
long: at least 32 bits
long long: at least 64 bits
Standard C does not specify that a long double must occupy a minimum number of bits, only that it occupies no fewer bits than a double.

const Qualifier
Any type can hold a constant value.
A constant value cannot be changed.
To qualify a type as holding a constant value we use the keyword const
A type qualified as const is unmodifiable.
If a program instruction attempts to modify a const qualified type, the compiler will report an error.

# slide16
Negative and Positive Values
Computers store negative integers using encoding schemes:
Two's complement notation,
One's complement notation, and
Sign magnitude notation.
All of these schemes represent non-negative integers identically.
The most popular scheme is two's complement.
To obtain the two's complement of an integer, we:
Flip the bits (1-complement)
Add one  2-complement

6. Mixing Data Types
Although the ALU does not perform operations on operands of differing data type directly, C compilers can interpret expressions that contain operands of differing data type.
If a binary expression contains operands of differing type, a C compiler changes the data type of one of the operands to match the other.
Data type hierarchy: double, float, long, int , char .

# slide58
6. Mixing Data Types (cont.)
Implicit Casting for the assignment
If the data type of the variable on the left side of an assignment operator differs from the data type of the right side operand, the compiler:
Promotes the right operand to the data type of the left operand if the left operand is of a higher data type than the right operand,
Truncates the right operand to the data type of the left operand if the left operand is of a lower data type than the right operand.

Questions.Title: Meaning of sizeof in C
Questions.Description: According to the slides, what does the operator sizeof(var/type) return?
Options: A. The address of the variable or code
B. The size in bytes occupied by a variable or type
C. The value currently stored in the variable
D. The number of characters in the variable name
Questions.Explanation: B is correct because the slide explicitly states that sizeof(var/type) returns the size (number of bytes) occupied by a variable or type. A describes the address operator &, not sizeof. C refers to reading a variable's value, and D is unrelated to C semantics.

Questions.Title: scanf and printf Parameters
Questions.Description: Which statement matches the parameter usage of scanf and printf shown in the slides?
Options: A. scanf uses a format string followed by addresses of data holders; printf uses a format string followed by variable values
B. scanf uses variable values only; printf uses addresses only
C. scanf and printf both require only addresses of variables
D. scanf prints output to the screen and printf reads input from the keyboard
Questions.Explanation: A is correct because the slide shows scanf("input format", &var1, &var2, ...) for input and printf("output format", var1, var2, ...) for output. B and C confuse the way these functions receive arguments, and D reverses their basic purposes.

Output.Title: Valid C Variable Naming Rule
Output.Description: Which variable name is valid according to the rules for naming variables in C shown in the slides?
Options: A. total_books
B. 2totalBooks
C. total books
D. int
Output.Explanation: A is correct because variable names may contain letters and underscores, and they must begin with a letter or underscore. B is invalid because names cannot begin with a digit. C is invalid because names cannot contain whitespaces. D is invalid because a variable name must not be a C reserved word.

Output.Title: Meaning of sizeof in C
Output.Description: According to the slides, what does the operator sizeof(var/type) return?
Options: A. The address of the variable
B. The size in bytes occupied by a variable or type
C. The value stored in the variable
D. The number of characters in the variable name
Output.Explanation: B is correct because the slide states that sizeof(var/type) returns the size (number of byte) occupied by a variable/type. A is the role of the address operator &, not sizeof. C is about reading a variable's value, and D is unrelated to C semantics.

Output.Title: scanf and printf Parameter Meaning
Output.Description: In the example format shown in the slides, which statement correctly describes how scanf and printf use their parameters?
Options: A. scanf uses the format string first and then addresses of data holders; printf uses the format string first and then variable values
B. scanf uses variable values only; printf uses addresses only
C. scanf and printf both require only addresses of variables
D. scanf prints output to the screen and printf reads input from the keyboard
Output.Explanation: A is correct because the slide shows scanf("input format", &var1, &var2, ...) for input and printf("output format", var1, var2, ...) for output. B and C confuse the roles of the functions and the use of addresses. D reverses the basic purposes of scanf and printf.

Output.Title: Division Result with Integer Operands
Output.Description: What is the result of the expression 10/3 according to the arithmetic operator examples in the slides?
Output.Explanation: A is correct because the slide explicitly shows z = 10/3; => 3 when both operands are integers. B is the result of 10.0/3, where the presence of a floating-point operand changes the type of the division. C is not the quotient of 10 divided by 3, and D is not the result of integer division here.

Output.Title: Choosing a Suitable Data Type for a Book ID
Output.Description: A library system needs to store a unique book ID such as 2345678901. Which data type is the most suitable choice from the types discussed in the slides?
Options: A. int
B. char
C. double
D. float
Output.Explanation: A is the best choice among the listed basic types because the chunks describe int as an integer type for whole-number values, while char is for a single character and float/double are floating-point types for real numbers. The task in the slide asks students to choose a suitable type for a unique ID, which is an integer-like value, not a fractional one.

questions.Title: Valid C Variable Naming Rule
questions.Description: Which variable name is valid according to the rules for naming variables in C shown in the slides?
Options: A. total_books
B. 2totalBooks
C. total books
D. int
questions.Explanation: A is correct because variable names may contain letters and underscores, and they must begin with a letter or underscore. B is invalid because names cannot begin with a digit. C is invalid because names cannot contain whitespaces. D is invalid because a variable name must not be a C reserved word.

questions.Title: Meaning of sizeof in C
questions.Description: According to the slides, what does the operator sizeof(var/type) return?
Options: A. The address of the variable
B. The size in bytes occupied by a variable or type
C. The value stored in the variable
D. The number of characters in the variable name
questions.Explanation: B is correct because the slide states that sizeof(var/type) returns the size (number of byte) occupied by a variable/type. A is the role of the address operator &, not sizeof. C is about reading a variable's value, and D is unrelated to C semantics.

questions.Title: scanf and printf Parameter Meaning
questions.Description: In the example format shown in the slides, which statement correctly describes how scanf and printf use their parameters?
Options: A. scanf uses the format string first and then addresses of data holders; printf uses the format string first and then variable values
B. scanf uses variable values only; printf uses addresses only
C. scanf and printf both require only addresses of variables
D. scanf prints output to the screen and printf reads input from the keyboard
questions.Explanation: A is correct because the slide shows scanf("input format", &var1, &var2, ...) for input and printf("output format", var1, var2, ...) for output. B and C confuse the roles of the functions and the use of addresses. D reverses the basic purposes of scanf and printf.

questions.Title: Division Result with Integer Operands
questions.Description: What is the result of the expression 10/3 according to the arithmetic operator examples in the slides?
questions.Explanation: A is correct because the slide explicitly shows z = 10/3; => 3 when both operands are integers. B is the result of 10.0/3, where the presence of a floating-point operand changes the type of the division. C is not the quotient of 10 divided by 3, and D is not the result of integer division here.

questions.Title: Choosing a Suitable Data Type for a Book ID
questions.Description: A library system needs to store a unique book ID such as 2345678901. Which data type is the most suitable choice from the types discussed in the slides?
Options: A. int
B. char
C. double
D. float
questions.Explanation: A is the best choice among the listed basic types because the chunks describe int as an integer type for whole-number values, while char is for a single character and float/double are floating-point types for real numbers. The task in the slide asks students to choose a suitable type for a unique ID, which is an integer-like value, not a fractional one.

Issues: One item has a direct answer-key contradiction: "Meaning of sizeof in C" marks option A as correct, but the explanation says B is correct. This makes the question invalid.
The set includes repeated low-level recall items centered on the same slide content (variable naming, sizeof, scanf/printf, integer division) without enough variety in reasoning demand.
Several topic tags include unrelated tags such as "class" and "pointer" for items that are primarily variables/data-type questions, which weakens rubric alignment.

The book ID question is only partially grounded: the slides discuss choosing suitable types for integer-like values, but they do not explicitly justify that a 10-digit ID must be stored in int across environments. The item would be safer if phrased more generally or supported with a clearer chunk match.

questions.Title: Valid C Variable Naming Rule
questions.Description: Which variable name is valid according to the rules for naming variables in C shown in the slides?
Options: A. total_books
B. 2totalBooks
C. total books
D. int
questions.Explanation: A is correct because variable names may contain letters and underscores, and they must begin with a letter or underscore. B is invalid because names cannot begin with a digit. C is invalid because names cannot contain whitespaces. D is invalid because a variable name must not be a C reserved word.

questions.Title: Meaning of sizeof in C
questions.Description: According to the slides, what does the operator sizeof(var/type) return?
Options: A. The address of the variable
B. The size in bytes occupied by a variable or type
C. The value stored in the variable
D. The number of characters in the variable name
questions.Explanation: B is correct because the slide states that sizeof(var/type) returns the size (number of byte) occupied by a variable/type. A is the role of the address operator &, not sizeof. C is about reading a variable's value, and D is unrelated to C semantics.

questions.Title: scanf and printf Parameter Meaning
questions.Description: In the example format shown in the slides, which statement correctly describes how scanf and printf use their parameters?
Options: A. scanf uses the format string first and then addresses of data holders; printf uses the format string first and then variable values
B. scanf uses variable values only; printf uses addresses only
C. scanf and printf both require only addresses of variables
D. scanf prints output to the screen and printf reads input from the keyboard
questions.Explanation: A is correct because the slide shows scanf("input format", &var1, &var2, ...) for input and printf("output format", var1, var2, ...) for output. B and C confuse the roles of the functions and the use of addresses. D reverses the basic purposes of scanf and printf.

questions.Title: Division Result with Integer Operands
questions.Description: What is the result of the expression 10/3 according to the arithmetic operator examples in the slides?
questions.Explanation: A is correct because the slide explicitly shows z = 10/3; => 3 when both operands are integers. B is the result of 10.0/3, where the presence of a floating-point operand changes the type of the division. C is not the quotient of 10 divided by 3, and D is not the result of integer division here.

questions.Title: Choosing a Suitable Data Type for a Book ID
questions.Description: A library system needs to store a unique book ID such as 2345678901. Which data type is the most suitable choice from the types discussed in the slides?
Options: A. int
B. char
C. double
D. float
questions.Explanation: A is the best choice among the listed basic types because the chunks describe int as an integer type for whole-number values, while char is for a single character and float/double are floating-point types for real numbers. The task in the slide asks students to choose a suitable type for a unique ID, which is an integer-like value, not a fractional one.

int Type Size Specifiers
Specifying the size of an int ensures that the type contains a minimum number of bits. The three specifiers are:
short: at least 16 bits
long: at least 32 bits
long long: at least 64 bits
Standard C does not specify that a long double must occupy a minimum number of bits, only that it occupies no fewer bits than a double.

Promotes the right operand to the data type of the left operand if the left operand is of a higher data type than the right operand,

previousQuestions.Title: Valid C Variable Naming Rule
previousQuestions.Description: Which variable name is valid according to the rules for naming variables in C shown in the slides?
Options: A. total_books
B. 2totalBooks
C. total books
D. int
previousQuestions.Explanation: A is correct because variable names may contain letters and underscores, and they must begin with a letter or underscore. B is invalid because names cannot begin with a digit. C is invalid because names cannot contain whitespaces. D is invalid because a variable name must not be a C reserved word.

previousQuestions.Title: Meaning of sizeof in C
previousQuestions.Description: According to the slides, what does the operator sizeof(var/type) return?
Options: A. The address of the variable
B. The size in bytes occupied by a variable or type
C. The value stored in the variable
D. The number of characters in the variable name
previousQuestions.Explanation: B is correct because the slide states that sizeof(var/type) returns the size (number of byte) occupied by a variable/type. A is the role of the address operator &, not sizeof. C is about reading a variable's value, and D is unrelated to C semantics.

previousQuestions.Title: scanf and printf Parameter Meaning
previousQuestions.Description: In the example format shown in the slides, which statement correctly describes how scanf and printf use their parameters?
Options: A. scanf uses the format string first and then addresses of data holders; printf uses the format string first and then variable values
B. scanf uses variable values only; printf uses addresses only
C. scanf and printf both require only addresses of variables
D. scanf prints output to the screen and printf reads input from the keyboard
previousQuestions.Explanation: A is correct because the slide shows scanf("input format", &var1, &var2, ...) for input and printf("output format", var1, var2, ...) for output. B and C confuse the roles of the functions and the use of addresses. D reverses the basic purposes of scanf and printf.

previousQuestions.Title: Division Result with Integer Operands
previousQuestions.Description: What is the result of the expression 10/3 according to the arithmetic operator examples in the slides?
previousQuestions.Explanation: A is correct because the slide explicitly shows z = 10/3; => 3 when both operands are integers. B is the result of 10.0/3, where the presence of a floating-point operand changes the type of the division. C is not the quotient of 10 divided by 3, and D is not the result of integer division here.

previousQuestions.Title: Choosing a Suitable Data Type for a Book ID
previousQuestions.Description: A library system needs to store a unique book ID such as 2345678901. Which data type is the most suitable choice from the types discussed in the slides?
Options: A. int
B. char
C. double
D. float
previousQuestions.Explanation: A is the best choice among the listed basic types because the chunks describe int as an integer type for whole-number values, while char is for a single character and float/double are floating-point types for real numbers. The task in the slide asks students to choose a suitable type for a unique ID, which is an integer-like value, not a fractional one.

Output.Title: Meaning of sizeof in C

Options: A. The address of the variable or code
B. The size in bytes occupied by a variable or type
C. The value currently stored in the variable
D. The number of characters in the variable name
Output.Explanation: B is correct because the slide explicitly states that sizeof(var/type) returns the size (number of bytes) occupied by a variable or type. A describes the address operator &, not sizeof. C refers to reading a variable's value, and D is unrelated to C semantics.

Output.Title: scanf and printf Parameters
Output.Description: Which statement matches the parameter usage of scanf and printf shown in the slides?
Options: A. scanf uses a format string followed by addresses of data holders; printf uses a format string followed by variable values
B. scanf uses variable values only; printf uses addresses only
C. scanf and printf both require only addresses of variables
D. scanf prints output to the screen and printf reads input from the keyboard
Output.Explanation: A is correct because the slide shows scanf("input format", &var1, &var2, ...) for input and printf("output format", var1, var2, ...) for output. B and C confuse the way these functions receive arguments, and D reverses their basic purposes.

Output.Title: Integer Division with Mixed Operands
Output.Description: What result does the slide imply for the expression 10.0/3?
Output.Explanation: B is correct because the slide shows that 10.0/3 gives 3.3333333. The presence of the floating-point literal 10.0 makes the division a real-number division. A is the integer-division result for 10/3, while C and D do not match the example.

Output.Title: Implicit Casting in Assignment
Output.Description: If a double value is assigned to an int variable, what does the slide say the compiler does?
Options: A. Promotes the int value to double before storing it
B. Truncates the double value to the int data type
C. Converts the int variable into a floating-point variable permanently
D. Reports that assignment between different data types is not allowed
Output.Explanation: B is correct because the slide states that if the left-side variable has a lower data type than the right-side operand, the compiler truncates the right operand to the type of the left operand. A is the opposite direction of promotion. C is not described in the slide, and D contradicts the slide's explanation of implicit casting.

Output.Title: Effect of const on Modification
Output.Description: What happens if a program instruction attempts to modify a const-qualified type?
Options: A. The value is updated normally because const only affects input
B. The compiler reports an error
C. The compiler automatically changes const into a non-const variable
D. The program prints a warning but still changes the value
Output.Explanation: B is correct because the slide says a const-qualified type is unmodifiable and that any attempt to modify it will cause a compiler error. A, C, and D contradict that rule in different ways.

# slide10
int Type Size Specifiers
Specifying the size of an int ensures that the type contains a minimum number of bits. The three specifiers are:
short: at least 16 bits
long: at least 32 bits
long long: at least 64 bits
Standard C does not specify that a long double must occupy a minimum number of bits, only that it occupies no fewer bits than a double.

double Type Size Specifier
The size of a long double depends on the environment and is typically at least 64 bits:
long double type only ensures that it contains at least as many bits as a double

# slide12
const Qualifier
Any type can hold a constant value.
A constant value cannot be changed.
To qualify a type as holding a constant value we use the keyword const
A type qualified as const is unmodifiable.
If a program instruction attempts to modify a const qualified type, the compiler will report an error.

Representing Values
Hardware manufacturers distinguish integral types from floating-point types and represent integral data and floating-point data differently.
Integral types: char, int
Floating-point types: float, double

Representation of Integral Values
C stores integral values in equivalent binary form.
Non-Negative Values:
Intel uses this little-endian ordering.
Motorola uses big-endian ordering.

09F5E103

Each CPU family has it’s own way to store data . So, compilers must have a suitable way for copying data from this variable to other. And due to this reason also, each compiler can run well only on a specific family of CPU only. A supplier may supply some versions of their compiler for some CPU families.

Negative and Positive Values
Computers store negative integers using encoding schemes:
Two's complement notation,
One's complement notation, and
Sign magnitude notation.

# slide24
Declaring (Creating) Variables
To create a variable, specify the data type and assign it a value:
Syntax:
For example:
char section
int numberOfClasses;
double cashFare = 2.25;

questions.Title: Meaning of sizeof in C
questions.Description: According to the slides, what does the operator sizeof(var/type) return?
Options: A. The address of the variable or code
B. The size in bytes occupied by a variable or type
C. The value currently stored in the variable
D. The number of characters in the variable name
questions.Explanation: B is correct because the slide explicitly states that sizeof(var/type) returns the size (number of bytes) occupied by a variable or type. A describes the address operator &, not sizeof. C refers to reading a variable's value, and D is unrelated to C semantics.

questions.Title: scanf and printf Parameters
questions.Description: Which statement matches the parameter usage of scanf and printf shown in the slides?
Options: A. scanf uses a format string followed by addresses of data holders; printf uses a format string followed by variable values
B. scanf uses variable values only; printf uses addresses only
C. scanf and printf both require only addresses of variables
D. scanf prints output to the screen and printf reads input from the keyboard
questions.Explanation: A is correct because the slide shows scanf("input format", &var1, &var2, ...) for input and printf("output format", var1, var2, ...) for output. B and C confuse the way these functions receive arguments, and D reverses their basic purposes.

questions.Title: Integer Division with Mixed Operands
questions.Description: What result does the slide imply for the expression 10.0/3?
questions.Explanation: B is correct because the slide shows that 10.0/3 gives 3.3333333. The presence of the floating-point literal 10.0 makes the division a real-number division. A is the integer-division result for 10/3, while C and D do not match the example.

questions.Title: Implicit Casting in Assignment
questions.Description: If a double value is assigned to an int variable, what does the slide say the compiler does?
Options: A. Promotes the int value to double before storing it
B. Truncates the double value to the int data type
C. Converts the int variable into a floating-point variable permanently
D. Reports that assignment between different data types is not allowed
questions.Explanation: B is correct because the slide states that if the left-side variable has a lower data type than the right-side operand, the compiler truncates the right operand to the type of the left operand. A is the opposite direction of promotion. C is not described in the slide, and D contradicts the slide's explanation of implicit casting.

questions.Title: Effect of const on Modification
questions.Description: What happens if a program instruction attempts to modify a const-qualified type?
Options: A. The value is updated normally because const only affects input
B. The compiler reports an error
C. The compiler automatically changes const into a non-const variable
D. The program prints a warning but still changes the value
questions.Explanation: B is correct because the slide says a const-qualified type is unmodifiable and that any attempt to modify it will cause a compiler error. A, C, and D contradict that rule in different ways.

# slide10
int Type Size Specifiers
Specifying the size of an int ensures that the type contains a minimum number of bits. The three specifiers are:
short: at least 16 bits
long: at least 32 bits
long long: at least 64 bits
Standard C does not specify that a long double must occupy a minimum number of bits, only that it occupies no fewer bits than a double.

# slide11
double Type Size Specifier
The size of a long double depends on the environment and is typically at least 64 bits:
long double type only ensures that it contains at least as many bits as a double

30/12/2024

# slide12
const Qualifier
Any type can hold a constant value.
A constant value cannot be changed.
To qualify a type as holding a constant value we use the keyword const
A type qualified as const is unmodifiable.
If a program instruction attempts to modify a const qualified type, the compiler will report an error.

# slide13
Representing Values
Hardware manufacturers distinguish integral types from floating-point types and represent integral data and floating-point data differently.
Integral types: char, int
Floating-point types: float, double

# slide14
Representation of Integral Values
C stores integral values in equivalent binary form.
Non-Negative Values:
Intel uses this little-endian ordering.
Motorola uses big-endian ordering.

Value is stored:
09F5E103
Least significant is stored in lowest byte

questions.Title: Meaning of sizeof in C
questions.Description: According to the slides, what does the operator sizeof(var/type) return?
Options: A. The address of the variable or code
B. The size in bytes occupied by a variable or type
C. The value currently stored in the variable
D. The number of characters in the variable name
questions.Explanation: B is correct because the slide explicitly states that sizeof(var/type) returns the size (number of bytes) occupied by a variable or type. A describes the address operator &, not sizeof. C refers to reading a variable's value, and D is unrelated to C semantics.

questions.Title: scanf and printf Parameters
questions.Description: Which statement matches the parameter usage of scanf and printf shown in the slides?
Options: A. scanf uses a format string followed by addresses of data holders; printf uses a format string followed by variable values
B. scanf uses variable values only; printf uses addresses only
C. scanf and printf both require only addresses of variables
D. scanf prints output to the screen and printf reads input from the keyboard
questions.Explanation: A is correct because the slide shows scanf("input format", &var1, &var2, ...) for input and printf("output format", var1, var2, ...) for output. B and C confuse the way these functions receive arguments, and D reverses their basic purposes.

questions.Title: Integer Division with Mixed Operands
questions.Description: What result does the slide imply for the expression 10.0/3?
questions.Explanation: B is correct because the slide shows that 10.0/3 gives 3.3333333. The presence of the floating-point literal 10.0 makes the division a real-number division. A is the integer-division result for 10/3, while C and D do not match the example.

questions.Title: Implicit Casting in Assignment
questions.Description: If a double value is assigned to an int variable, what does the slide say the compiler does?
Options: A. Promotes the int value to double before storing it
B. Truncates the double value to the int data type
C. Converts the int variable into a floating-point variable permanently
D. Reports that assignment between different data types is not allowed
questions.Explanation: B is correct because the slide states that if the left-side variable has a lower data type than the right-side operand, the compiler truncates the right operand to the type of the left operand. A is the opposite direction of promotion. C is not described in the slide, and D contradicts the slide's explanation of implicit casting.

questions.Title: Effect of const on Modification
questions.Description: What happens if a program instruction attempts to modify a const-qualified type?
Options: A. The value is updated normally because const only affects input
B. The compiler reports an error
C. The compiler automatically changes const into a non-const variable
D. The program prints a warning but still changes the value

institution_context.target_students: FPT University students in foundational programming courses

easy.description: Single-concept recall or direct interpretation questions about basic C syntax or semantics.
expected_skills: Identify variable, data type, operator, or control-flow behavior.
Recognize simple array, loop, function, or pointer basics.
Answer without multi-step tracing or deep debugging.

expected_skills: Trace loops, arrays, or function calls.
Reason about pointer usage at a basic to intermediate level.
Detect common semantic mistakes or output behavior.
should_avoid: Advanced undefined behavior traps that are not grounded in the source material.

hard.description: Questions requiring careful code tracing, deeper semantic understanding, or subtle reasoning about pointers, arrays, functions, or memory behavior.
expected_skills: Differentiate close distractors based on true C semantics.
Reason about non-trivial pointer or array behavior if grounded in the chunks.
should_avoid: Topics not present in introductory C course material.

The question must stay within introductory C scope.

easy: Requires multi-step tracing across several statements or functions.
Uses tricky pointer semantics that exceed beginner recall.
Includes distractors that require advanced edge-case knowledge.
medium: Can be answered by direct definition recall only.
Depends on content absent from the chunks.
hard: Only tests a single factual definition.
Does not require meaningful reasoning beyond beginner recall.
